slides.title: Radiation, dose, + biological effect
slides.body:
**Ionizing radiation** types:
• **Alpha (α)**: He-4 nuclei. Stopped by paper / skin. Dangerous internally (inhaled, ingested).
• **Beta (β)**: high-energy electrons. Stopped by aluminum. Skin burn risk; internal hazard moderate.
• **Gamma (γ)**: high-energy photons. Penetrating; require Pb / steel shielding.
• **Neutrons**: from fission + activated materials. Require hydrogenous shielding (water, polyethylene).
• **X-rays**: similar to γ.

**Units**:
• **Activity**: Bq (1/s) or Ci (3.7×10¹⁰ Bq). Decays per second.
• **Absorbed dose**: Gy (J/kg) or rad (0.01 Gy). Energy deposited.
• **Equivalent dose**: Sv or rem (0.01 Sv). Absorbed dose × radiation weighting factor (α=20, β=γ=1, neutrons=5-20).
• **Effective dose**: Sv. Equivalent × tissue weighting (gonads ×0.2, bone marrow ×0.12, lung ×0.12, etc.) for whole-body risk.

**Background**: ~2.4 mSv/yr natural (radon + cosmic + internal + terrestrial). + ~3 mSv/yr medical (CT scans dominant). Total ~5 mSv/yr average.

**Dose limits (US, NRC + DOE)**:
• Public: 1 mSv/yr (~5× medical CT).
• Worker: 50 mSv/yr (50× public). Pregnant worker: 5 mSv during pregnancy.
• Emergency response: ~250 mSv if necessary to save lives.

**Acute high doses**:
• 0.5-1 Sv: ARS symptoms (nausea, fatigue).
• 4-5 Sv: ~50% mortality without treatment.
• 10+ Sv: nearly always fatal.

**Chronic (low) dose** + cancer: linear-no-threshold (LNT) hypothesis: cancer risk ~5% per Sv. Controversial at low doses — some evidence for hormesis (small doses beneficial); regulatory uses LNT for conservatism. Actual cancer risk at <100 mSv extremely hard to measure (background ~25% lifetime cancer rate; 1 mSv adds ~0.005%).

slides.title: ALARA + the 3 R principles
slides.body:
**ALARA**: As Low As Reasonably Achievable. Federal + ICRP principle for occupational exposure.

Not 'zero' (impractical + expensive) but 'as low as reasonable.' Reasonableness includes cost, time, complexity. Modern reactor workers average ~1-2 mSv/yr; refueling personnel can reach 5-10 mSv.

**3 R's of radiation protection**:
1. **Time**: minimize exposure duration. Dose ∝ time.
2. **Distance**: dose decreases with 1/r² (point source). Doubling distance → 1/4 dose.
3. **Shielding**: absorbs radiation. Lead (γ), polyethylene/water (n), aluminum (β).

**Operational practices**:
• Work-permit system; pre-job briefing on dose budget.
• Personal dosimeters (TLD, EPD, optically-stimulated luminescence).
• Time + dose tracking; supervisor alerts at thresholds.
• Engineering controls: remote handling tools, robotic systems, fixed shielding.
• Procedures: rotation of personnel, dry runs, mock-ups.

**Hot cell** operations: heavily shielded chambers with remote manipulators (master-slave or telerobotic). Used for reprocessing, R&D, decommissioning. Operators outside cell; observe via leaded glass + cameras.

**Radiation areas** classification:
- Unrestricted area: <0.02 mSv/h
- Controlled area: 0.02-1 mSv/h
- Radiation area: 0.05-1 mSv/h
- High radiation area: >1 mSv/h
- Very-high radiation area: >5 Gy/h (e.g., spent-fuel pool surface, hot cell)

Modern reactors: most operating areas <1 µSv/h; only specific work activities at higher levels.

slides.title: Major accident case studies + lessons
slides.body:
**Three Mile Island Unit 2 (Mar 28, 1979, US)**:
- Cause: pilot-operated relief valve (PORV) stuck open after a feedwater pump trip. Coolant leaked; operators throttled HPI ECCS due to misread indications. Core uncovered + partially melted (~50%).
- Release: minimal — containment held. ~93 PBq Xe + Kr noble gases vented. Estimated max offsite dose: ~0.5 mSv.
- Deaths: 0 (directly attributable).
- Lessons: operator training (industry-wide simulator program), procedures (symptom-based), control room design, regulatory restructuring (NRC strengthened), public communication.

**Chernobyl Unit 4 (Apr 26, 1986, USSR/Ukraine)**:
- Cause: experiment outside safe envelope + RBMK design flaws (positive void coefficient + graphite-tipped control rods) → prompt-critical excursion → steam + hydrogen explosion + graphite fire (10 days).
- Release: ~5300 PBq of radioactive material — largest civilian release ever. Cs-137, I-131, Sr-90 dispersed across Europe.
- Deaths: ~28 acute radiation deaths (firefighters + operators). ~15 thyroid-cancer deaths in children (treatable but deadly without). Estimated long-term cancers: ~4000-9000 excess deaths (WHO/IAEA). Other studies higher (TORCH ~30K-60K).
- ~150,000+ evacuated; 1000 km² exclusion zone. New Safe Confinement (NSC) installed 2016, 100-yr design.
- Lessons: design (no positive void; no positive control rod insertion); safety culture; international cooperation (IAEA strengthened); WANO created.

**Fukushima Daiichi (Mar 11, 2011, Japan)**:
- Cause: 9.1 earthquake + 13-15 m tsunami flooded backup diesels at 4 of 6 BWR units. Loss of decay-heat removal → fuel melt in 3 units → H₂ explosions in reactor buildings.
- Release: ~520 PBq (1/10 of Chernobyl). Ocean release also significant.
- Deaths: 0 acute radiation deaths. 1 worker died of radiation-attributable cancer (lung, 2018). ~50 deaths from evacuation stress + interrupted medical care. Estimated long-term cancers: low single-digit thousands (range; LNT-extrapolation contested).
- ~150,000 evacuated; ~25 km² exclusion zone (much smaller than Chernobyl; better containment + less explosive release).
- Lessons: external-hazard envelopes (seismic + flood); common-mode failures; passive cooling; portable equipment (FLEX); long-term beyond-design-basis station blackout; spent-fuel pool resilience.

**Aggregate lessons across all accidents**:
1. Defense in depth: multiple, *diverse* barriers (not just redundant).
2. Safety culture: ongoing training, near-miss reporting, just culture.
3. International cooperation: WANO + IAEA assistance, peer review, transparent reporting.
4. Designs that fail safe: inherent + passive safety eliminating need for active intervention.
5. Public communication + emergency response planning.
6. Continuous learning: every event → industry-wide updates.

Modern Gen III+ designs (AP1000, EPR, ESBWR, etc.) explicitly address all three accident scenarios with engineered + procedural improvements.

question.question: Estimate dose received during a typical industrial radiography job
question.goal: An industrial radiographer uses an Ir-192 source (activity 3.7×10¹² Bq = 100 Ci, average γ energy 0.38 MeV). Calculate dose rate at 1 m from unshielded source, then evaluate operator dose for a 5-minute exposure at 3 m distance behind 2 cm steel shielding (attenuation factor 10).

steps.prompt: Approximate γ exposure rate per Bq at 1 m for Ir-192?
hints: Ir-192 specific gamma constant ≈ 0.13 mSv/h per Ci at 1 m.
steps.reveal: Ir-192 specific γ constant Γ ≈ 0.13 mSv/h per Ci at 1 m.

steps.prompt: Dose rate at 1 m from 100 Ci source?
steps.reveal: 13 mSv/h at 1 m from 100 Ci Ir-192 unshielded. Lethal dose (5 Sv) in ~6 hr at this distance!

steps.prompt: Apply distance shielding (3 m vs 1 m, 1/r²)?

steps.reveal: Behind 2 cm steel + at 3 m: 0.14 mSv/h ≈ 140 µSv/h.

~12 µSv per 5-min job. Annual radiographer dose budget: ~50 mSv → ~4000 such operations per year. ALARA: increase distance + shield further to lower dose; rotate personnel; ensure each operation as quick + far as practical. Real-world radiographers average ~5-10 mSv/yr; high-end operators (e.g., pipeline radiography in oil + gas) can approach 20-30 mSv/yr. All within regulatory limits but practiced ALARA.

question.question: Why do the casualty estimates for Chernobyl + Fukushima vary so widely across studies?
options: Cancer fatalities from low-dose radiation can only be statistically inferred; individual cases aren't attributable. Studies differ on: (1) dose-response model (LNT vs threshold vs hormesis); (2) which dose categories to count (acute vs chronic, internal vs external, low-dose vs high-dose); (3) populations considered (worker, evacuee, general public, nearby vs far); (4) follow-up duration (decades for solid cancers); (5) baseline cancer rate uncertainty. Chernobyl: ~28 direct + ~15 thyroid cancer + 4000-60000 statistical depending on model. Fukushima: 0 direct + ~thousands statistical (heavily contested).
question.explanation:
**Why radiation casualty estimates vary**:

*Direct vs statistical*: only acute high-dose deaths (>~1 Sv whole-body) are individually attributable. Chronic / low-dose / cancer deaths are *statistical* — population-level excess above baseline.

*Baseline*: cancer is the second-leading cause of death in industrialized countries (~25% lifetime risk). Adding ~0.5% statistical risk from 100 mSv vs baseline 25% is impossible to identify individually.

*Dose-response model* (the biggest variable):
- **LNT (Linear No-Threshold)**: cancer risk linear with dose, no threshold. ICRP, BEIR VII, regulatory default. Mathematically simple, conservative. Critics argue it overestimates at low dose.
- **Threshold**: no risk below threshold (e.g., 100 mSv). Cancer suppression at very low doses observed in some studies. UNSCEAR analyses sometimes adopt.
- **Hormesis**: low doses beneficial. Some studies show DNA repair stimulation; controversial; not regulatory consensus.

*Methodological choices*:
- Worker doses: well-documented in registries.
- Public doses: estimated via fallout maps + biokinetic modeling — large uncertainties.
- Internal vs external: different biokinetic + radiotoxicity.
- Follow-up duration: solid cancers can take 30-50 yr to manifest after exposure.
- Confounders: tobacco, occupational, evacuation stress, medical history.

*Specific accident estimates*:

**Chernobyl**:
- Direct deaths: ~28 (ARS, firefighters, operators); ~15 children with thyroid cancer (treatable with surgery + I-131 ablation but require lifelong levothyroxine).
- WHO/IAEA Chernobyl Forum (2005): up to 4000 excess deaths.
- TORCH (2006, Greenpeace-commissioned): 30,000-60,000.
- Yablokov+ (2009): 985,000 (heavily criticized methodology).
- IAEA 2018 update: consistent with 4000-9000.
- Honestly: the LNT-extrapolated number is highly uncertain at low doses; actual measured excess cancers in evacuee populations have been only slightly above baseline statistically.

**Fukushima**:
- Direct radiation deaths: 0 acute. 1 cancer death (2018, lung — partially attributed).
- Evacuation-related deaths: ~50 (stress, interrupted care).
- Predicted statistical cancers: ~100-1000 (UNSCEAR 2013, low end given lower releases than Chernobyl).
- Some studies predict 0 detectable excess given low absolute doses (most evacuees <5 mSv).

**Key insight**: the *evacuation* often causes more health impact than the radiation in many scenarios (especially low-dose). Risk-communication + emergency-response planning increasingly include this tradeoff.

**Conclusion**: 'How many people died from Chernobyl?' has no single answer because individual attribution at low doses is impossible. Statistical excess varies with dose-response model + methodology. This is genuine uncertainty, not denial or coverup.

slides.workedSolution: Low-dose cancers only statistically attributable; individual cases lost in background (25% lifetime cancer rate). Estimates depend on: dose-response model (LNT vs threshold vs hormesis); dose categories (acute/chronic, internal/external); populations; follow-up duration. Chernobyl: ~28 direct + ~15 thyroid + 4000-60000 statistical (LNT). Fukushima: 0 acute + thousands statistical (or near-zero if threshold model). Genuine methodological uncertainty, not denial. Often evacuation causes more harm than radiation.

question.question: Why does the linear-no-threshold (LNT) hypothesis remain controversial in radiation protection?
options: LNT extrapolates high-dose effects (well-measured in atomic-bomb survivors at 1+ Sv) linearly down to low doses (<100 mSv) where measurement is impossible. Critics argue: (1) DNA repair mechanisms may suppress damage at low dose; (2) hormesis (small benefit) observed in some experiments; (3) cellular adaptive response not captured. Defenders: conservative for regulation; consistent with mechanistic understanding (single mutation can initiate cancer); precautionary principle. ICRP, BEIR, regulatory bodies continue to use LNT pending stronger contrary evidence. Active research area.
LNT only applies to medical CT scans.
question.explanation:
**LNT (Linear No-Threshold)** hypothesis: cancer risk is proportional to absorbed dose, with no lower threshold. Implications: 1 person at 1 Sv → 1 cancer; 1000 people at 1 mSv → 1 cancer. Doses sum linearly.

*Evidence base*:
- **Atomic-bomb survivors** (Life Span Study, ~90K survivors, follow-up 1950-present): well-documented dose-response for solid cancers down to ~100 mSv. Linear at high dose.
- **Medical radiation workers**: dose-response data, much lower doses.
- **Mayak / Techa River workers** (USSR): dose-response data.
- **Animal studies**: extensive at all dose ranges; some show suppression / hormesis at very low doses.
- **Cellular + molecular studies**: DNA damage + repair mechanisms; mutation rates; adaptive response.

*LNT extrapolation*:
The atomic-bomb data is robust above ~100 mSv. Below that, statistical power vanishes (need millions of subjects to detect tiny excess against ~25% baseline cancer rate). LNT *extrapolates* the high-dose linear fit down to zero.

*Critics' arguments*:
1. **Biological non-linearity**: at low doses, DNA repair + cellular adaptive responses + immune surveillance may eliminate damage before mutations accumulate. Mechanistically distinct from high-dose damage.
2. **Hormesis observations**: some animal + epidemiological studies show low-dose stimulation of repair → net benefit. Examples: chronic low-dose workers having lower cancer than controls (selection-biased? hormesis?).
3. **Threshold models**: alternative models with threshold (e.g., 100 mSv) fit data equally well + are mechanistically plausible.
4. **Practical**: LNT-based regulation gives huge weight to tiny doses that may have no effect → wasted resources on radiation protection rather than other risks.

*Defenders' arguments*:
1. **Conservatism**: LNT errs toward protection. Tail-risk asymmetry favors over- vs under-protection.
2. **Mechanistic plausibility**: single mutation can initiate cancer; no logical 'safe' threshold for stochastic damage.
3. **Regulatory simplicity**: LNT is mathematically tractable; thresholds vary across cell type + age + sex.
4. **Population-scale**: at large populations × small doses, even tiny per-capita risk yields measurable casualty counts; doesn't matter at individual level.

*Regulatory consensus*: ICRP (International Commission on Radiological Protection), BEIR (National Academy), UNSCEAR, IAEA, NRC all continue using LNT for radiation protection. They acknowledge uncertainty at low doses but treat as default.

*Active research*:
- **EU's Million-Person Study** (occupational): more statistical power at low doses.
- **Mayak workers + Chernobyl evacuees**: long-term follow-up.
- **Animal + cellular models**: mechanism-of-action studies.

*Practical impact*:
- Medical CT scans: LNT predicts ~1-10 cancer / 1000 CTs (population scale). Critics: actual measurable is near-zero.
- Workplace dose limits: ~10× more conservative under LNT than under threshold models.
- Accident response: evacuation triggers + dose-budget allocation depend on LNT.

The field remains divided. Most working scientists agree LNT is the best available default for regulation but recognize it likely overestimates at very low doses. Future epidemiology may sharpen this — meanwhile, LNT remains the conservative working hypothesis.

slides.workedSolution: LNT extrapolates linear dose-response (well-measured >100 mSv in atomic-bomb survivors) down to zero. Below 100 mSv, statistical power fails. Critics: DNA repair + adaptive response + hormesis suggest sublinear at low dose. Defenders: conservatism + mechanistic plausibility + regulatory simplicity. Active research in occupational + accident epidemiology + cellular biology. Consensus: LNT is regulatory default but acknowledged as likely conservative at low dose. Field remains genuinely uncertain at <100 mSv.

question.question: A radiation source produces 100 µSv/h at 1 m. What's the dose rate at 5 m (point source, inverse-square law)?

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain to a worried neighbor why low-dose radiation exposure (e.g., living near a normally-operating nuclear plant) is not a meaningful health concern.
question.rubric: Mentions: typical plant boundary doses ~10-100 µSv/yr — about 1-5% of natural background (~3 mSv/yr). Background + medical scans are dominant exposure sources; living near a normally-operating plant adds negligibly. LNT-extrapolated risk: ~0.005% per mSv lifetime cancer → essentially indistinguishable from baseline 25% lifetime cancer. Accident risk: modern Gen III+ plants have core-damage frequency ~10⁻⁵/yr × release probability conditional on core damage ~10% → ~10⁻⁶/yr; far lower than other societal risks. Conservatively LNT-based regulation already accounts for worst case. Compare to: smoking (10-30× background dose equivalent in cancer risk), CT scans (1-10 mSv per scan), air travel (~0.05 mSv per long flight). Acknowledge legitimate concerns (waste, accident planning, transparency) without medical fear. Concludes: low-dose radiation from normal nuclear operation is not a real-world health concern compared to other modifiable risks.
